The Stakes of Fantasy Football¶

Fantasy football has grown from a niche hobby into a mainstream part of how millions of Americans watch the NFL. Research presented by the Fantasy Sports & Gaming Association at its 2025 Summer Conference estimated that roughly 53 million American adults played a fantasy sport in the past year, with football drawing by far the largest share of that audience. For a lot of those players, the weekly lineup decision is treated as a genuine analytical problem, not a guess. Which stats actually predict scoring, and which are just noise?

I currently manage rosters in three separate fantasy football leagues, so this project is a chance to test some of my own long-held assumptions directly against real data instead of gut feel or league-mate folklore: does raw usage (targets, carries) really predict fantasy production the way conventional wisdom says it does? Are some positions genuinely more predictable than others? Six full seasons of verified NFL outcomes is enough data to actually answer those questions instead of just guessing at them.

About the Data¶

For this project I used weekly player performance data from nflverse, an open-source project that aggregates and republishes official NFL statistics built on play-by-play data. The specific release used here, stats_player, provides one row per player per week and covers passing, rushing, receiving, kicking, punting, and individual defensive statistics: 150 columns in total, spanning every position on a roster, not just offensive skill positions.

I pulled six full regular seasons, 2020 through 2025, for a combined 112,450 player-week rows before any filtering. Because the raw file mixes every position together, the first real task is narrowing it down to the rows that are actually relevant to standard offensive fantasy scoring: quarterback, running back, wide receiver, tight end, and kicker. That's where the analysis below begins.

Data Loading and Background¶

Importing Libraries and Loading the Data¶

Below are the standard libraries needed to load, manipulate, and visualize this data: pandas and numpy for data handling, and matplotlib for the charts throughout this notebook. The data itself is pulled directly from nflverse's public GitHub release rather than a local file, so this notebook can be re-run from scratch by anyone.

In [ ]:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

BASE_URL = "https://github.com/nflverse/nflverse-data/releases/download/stats_player/stats_player_week_{}.csv"

seasons = range(2020, 2026)  # 2020-2025
frames = []

for year in seasons:
    url = BASE_URL.format(year)
    df_year = pd.read_csv(url, low_memory=False)
    frames.append(df_year)
    print(f"{year}: {df_year.shape[0]} rows loaded")

df_all = pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True)
print(f"\nCombined shape: {df_all.shape}")
print(f"Seasons included: {sorted(df_all['season'].unique())}")

2020: 17602 rows loaded
2021: 18969 rows loaded
2022: 18831 rows loaded
2023: 18643 rows loaded
2024: 18983 rows loaded
2025: 19422 rows loaded

Combined shape: (112450, 150)
Seasons included: [2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025]

150 columns and 112,450 rows loaded across six seasons. 2020 loaded noticeably fewer rows than every other season (17,602 vs. roughly 18,700–19,400) because 2020 was the last 16-game NFL regular season; the league didn't expand to 17 games until 2021. The DtypeWarning some environments raise on fg_missed_list/fg_blocked_list is expected. Those columns hold text for kickers and nothing at all for everyone else, so pandas can't confidently guess a single dtype across 100k+ rows without help. It is not a sign of damaged data.

Narrowing to Fantasy-Relevant Rows¶

The raw pull includes individual defensive stats, punting, and other data that has nothing to do with standard fantasy scoring. Narrowing to regular-season games and the positions that actually score offensive fantasy points (quarterback, running back, wide receiver, tight end, and kicker) makes the dataset both smaller and far more directly usable.

In [ ]:
df_fantasy = df_all[
    (df_all['position'].isin(['QB', 'RB', 'WR', 'TE', 'K'])) &
    (df_all['season_type'] == 'REG')
].copy()

print(f"Fantasy-relevant rows: {df_fantasy.shape[0]}")
print(df_fantasy.isnull().sum().sort_values(ascending=False).head(10))

Fantasy-relevant rows: 38146
pt_long            38131
fg_blocked_list    38035
fg_missed_list     37410
fg_long            35472
fg_made_list       35472
fg_pct             35303
pat_pct            35230
passing_cpoe       34263
pacr               34247
passing_epa        34179
dtype: int64

That leaves 38,146 player-week rows. The missing-value list is worth reading carefully before assuming anything is broken: every column at the top, pt_long, fg_pct, pat_pct, pacr, passing_epa, is a rate or "longest-of" statistic that is mathematically undefined when a player recorded zero attempts that week, not a data-entry mistake. This distinction drives a lot of the cleaning decisions later in this notebook: counting stats (yards, receptions, carries) are filled with 0 when they don't apply; rate stats are correctly left as NaN.

Initial Descriptive Statistics and Visualization¶

Fantasy Scoring by Position, Before Cleaning¶

What does a typical fantasy performance look like at each position? A groupby on position, before any cleaning, gives a first read on the shape of the data.

In [ ]:
df_fantasy.groupby('position')['fantasy_points_ppr'].agg(
    ['count','mean','median','std','min','max']).round(2)
Out[ ]:
count mean median std min max
position

QB 3901 13.80 13.82 9.24 -5.74 51.88

In [ ]:
order = ['QB','RB','WR','TE','K']
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8,5.5))
data = [df_fantasy[df_fantasy['position']==p]['fantasy_points_ppr'].values for p in order]
ax.boxplot(data, tick_labels=order, patch_artist=True,
           flierprops=dict(marker='o', markersize=3, alpha=0.35, markerfacecolor='#888'))
ax.set_ylabel('PPR fantasy points (single game)')
ax.set_title('PPR Fantasy Points by Position: Raw, Before Cleaning')
ax.axhline(0, color='gray', linewidth=0.7, linestyle='--')
ax.grid(axis='y', alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Something here is broken, and it isn't the data. It's the column being trusted. Every kicker recorded a mean, median, and max fantasy score of essentially zero (max = 0.60 across 3,227 games), which is obviously wrong; kickers score real points on field goals every week. That flags fantasy_points_ppr for closer inspection in the cleaning section below, rather than trusting it blindly for every position. Everywhere else, the mean sits comfortably above the median at every position, classic right skew, exactly what would be expected from box-score data: most players have a quiet week, and a smaller number have a big one that pulls the average up.

Usage and Production for Wide Receivers and Tight Ends¶

Fantasy football wisdom says usage predicts production: the more touches a player gets, the more fantasy points he scores. That assumption can be tested directly with a correlation and a scatterplot.

In [ ]:
catchers = df_fantasy[df_fantasy['position'].isin(['WR','TE'])]
rb = df_fantasy[df_fantasy['position']=='RB']

r_targets = catchers['targets'].corr(catchers['fantasy_points_ppr'])
r_yards = catchers['receiving_yards'].corr(catchers['fantasy_points_ppr'])
r_carries = rb['carries'].corr(rb['fantasy_points_ppr'])

print(f"targets vs PPR points (WR/TE, n={len(catchers)}):        r = {r_targets:.3f}")
print(f"receiving_yards vs PPR points (WR/TE, n={len(catchers)}): r = {r_yards:.3f}")
print(f"carries vs PPR points (RB, n={len(rb)}):                 r = {r_carries:.3f}")

targets vs PPR points (WR/TE, n=21859):        r = 0.806
receiving_yards vs PPR points (WR/TE, n=21859): r = 0.914
carries vs PPR points (RB, n=9159):                 r = 0.752
In [ ]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7,5.5))
sample = catchers.sample(1500, random_state=1)
ax.scatter(sample['targets'], sample['fantasy_points_ppr'], alpha=0.25, s=15, color='#4C72B0')
z = np.polyfit(catchers['targets'], catchers['fantasy_points_ppr'], 1)
xs = np.linspace(0, catchers['targets'].max(), 50)
ax.plot(xs, np.polyval(z, xs), color='#C44E52', linewidth=2, label=f'linear fit (r={r_targets:.2f})')
ax.set_xlabel('Targets in game')
ax.set_ylabel('PPR fantasy points')
ax.set_title(f'Targets vs. PPR Fantasy Points: WR/TE, 2020–2025\n(n=1,500 sample of {len(catchers):,})')
ax.legend()
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Volume drives production, but it isn't the whole story. Receiving yards correlate with PPR points even tighter (r = 0.914) than targets do (r = 0.806), because yards feed almost directly into the scoring formula, while a target is one step removed. It has to convert into a catch, and then into yards or a touchdown, before it becomes points. That is exactly what the scatter shows: the cloud widens as targets increase, because two players getting 8 targets in the same week can still land anywhere from 5 to 25 points depending on how efficiently they turned those targets into production. Opportunity sets the floor; efficiency and big plays decide who wins the week.

Usage and Production for Running Backs¶

Does the same opportunity-to-production relationship hold for running backs, or does carry volume behave differently than targets do?

In [ ]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7,5.5))
sample = rb.sample(1500, random_state=2)
ax.scatter(sample['carries'], sample['fantasy_points_ppr'], alpha=0.25, s=15, color='#DD8452')
z = np.polyfit(rb['carries'], rb['fantasy_points_ppr'], 1)
xs = np.linspace(0, rb['carries'].max(), 50)
ax.plot(xs, np.polyval(z, xs), color='#4C72B0', linewidth=2, label=f'linear fit (r={r_carries:.2f})')
ax.set_xlabel('Carries in game')
ax.set_ylabel('PPR fantasy points')
ax.set_title(f'Carries vs. PPR Fantasy Points: RB, 2020–2025\n(n=1,500 sample of {len(rb):,})')
ax.legend()
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Same shape, slightly weaker relationship (r = 0.752 vs. 0.806 for targets). That gap makes sense: a running back's carries include short-yardage and goal-line work that isn't very efficient on a per-carry basis, and PPR scoring specifically rewards receiving work that most feature backs also do on the side, production the carries column doesn't capture at all. Carries alone undercount a modern receiving back's total opportunity.

Receiving Efficiency Correlations¶

Targets are just one piece of the receiving picture. How do targets, catches, yards, yards after the catch, and touchdowns all relate to each other and to fantasy points at the same time?

In [ ]:
cols = ['targets','receptions','receiving_yards','receiving_air_yards',
        'receiving_yards_after_catch','receiving_tds','fantasy_points_ppr']
catchers[cols].corr().round(2)

targets receptions receiving_yards receiving_air_yards receiving_yards_after_catch receiving_tds fantasy_points_ppr
targets 1.00 0.91 0.80 0.81 0.64 0.35 0.81
receptions 0.91 1.00 0.86 0.65 0.71 0.40 0.88
receiving_yards 0.80 0.86 1.00 0.74 0.78 0.44 0.91
receiving_air_yards 0.81 0.65 0.74 1.00 0.39 0.33 0.68
receiving_yards_after_catch 0.64 0.71 0.78 0.39 1.00 0.32 0.72
receiving_tds 0.35 0.40 0.44 0.33 0.32 1.00 0.71

In [ ]:
corr = catchers[cols].corr().round(2)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5,6.5))
im = ax.imshow(corr.values, cmap='RdBu_r', vmin=-1, vmax=1)
ax.set_xticks(range(len(cols))); ax.set_xticklabels(cols, rotation=45, ha='right')
ax.set_yticks(range(len(cols))); ax.set_yticklabels(cols)
for i in range(len(cols)):
    for j in range(len(cols)):
        ax.text(j, i, f"{corr.values[i,j]:.2f}", ha='center', va='center',
                color='white' if abs(corr.values[i,j])>0.6 else 'black', fontsize=8)
ax.set_title('Correlation Heatmap: WR/TE Receiving Stats vs. PPR Points')
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.8, label='Pearson r')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The most interesting number in this whole grid is receiving_tds. It barely correlates with the volume stats (0.35 with targets, 0.44 with receiving yards), far weaker than those stats correlate with each other. But it still correlates 0.71 with fantasy points, almost as strongly as targets does. Touchdowns are the least predictable part of a receiver's stat line and yet a huge share of his scoring swing, which is exactly why an efficient, high-volume player can still have a quiet week with no touchdown luck, and a low-volume player can have a huge one on two scores from four targets. This is the statistical root of the "boom-or-bust" idea explored later in this notebook.

Cleaning and Reorganizing the Data¶

Checking for Invalid or Duplicate Entries¶

Before making any cleaning decisions, it's worth checking whether this dataset actually contains errors, impossible stat lines or duplicated rows, the way a genuinely damaged dataset would.

In [ ]:
print("completions > attempts:", (df_fantasy['completions']>df_fantasy['attempts']).sum())
print("receptions > targets:  ", (df_fantasy['receptions']>df_fantasy['targets']).sum())
print("duplicate player-season-week rows:", df_fantasy.duplicated(subset=['player_id','season','week'], keep=False).sum())
print("null team or opponent fields:", df_fantasy[['team','opponent_team']].isnull().sum().sum())

completions > attempts: 0
receptions > targets:   0
duplicate player-season-week rows: 0
null team or opponent fields: 0

All four checks come back at zero. Unlike a lot of real-world data, this file doesn't contain corrupted rows to strip out; nflverse is a well-maintained official data pipeline, and it shows. The actual cleaning decisions that follow are about which valid rows and columns belong in this specific analysis, not about repairing broken ones.

Removing Kickers from the Analysis¶

The boxplot above showed every kicker scoring essentially zero fantasy points, which doesn't match reality. It's worth confirming that directly before deciding what to do about it.

In [ ]:
nonzero_k = (df_fantasy[df_fantasy['position']=='K']['fantasy_points_ppr']!=0).sum()
total_k = (df_fantasy['position']=='K').sum()
print(f"K rows with nonzero fantasy_points_ppr: {nonzero_k} of {total_k}")

df_clean = df_fantasy[df_fantasy['position'] != 'K'].copy()
print(f"Rows after dropping K: {len(df_clean)} (was {len(df_fantasy)})")

K rows with nonzero fantasy_points_ppr: 1 of 3227
Rows after dropping K: 34919 (was 38146)

3,226 of 3,227 kicker-games read exactly 0.00 for fantasy_points_ppr. The column simply doesn't score kicking. It isn't a case of missing or damaged rows, it's a case of a column not covering the position at all. Kickers aren't bad data; they're just not answerable with this particular field, so they're dropped from the fantasy-scoring analysis rather than left in to silently suggest kickers never score.

Handling Structural Missing Values¶

With kickers removed, it's worth confirming that the remaining missing values are still the same kind of structural, expected pattern seen earlier, not something that needs filling in.

In [ ]:
print(f"fg_pct null rate with kickers removed: {df_clean['fg_pct'].isna().mean():.1%}")
print(f"passing_epa null rate with kickers removed: {df_clean['passing_epa'].isna().mean():.1%}")

fg_pct null rate with kickers removed: 100.0%
passing_epa null rate with kickers removed: 88.6%

fg_pct is now null for literally every remaining row, which makes complete sense: no quarterback, running back, wide receiver, or tight end ever attempts a field goal, so the column is undefined for all of them. passing_epa is null for 88.6% of rows, which lines up almost exactly with the fact that only quarterbacks (about 11% of the remaining rows) ever attempt a pass. These are decisively not filled with 0 anywhere in this notebook. A 0% field-goal rate implies a missed kick, not the complete absence of an attempt, so filling it would fabricate information that was never there.

Retaining Zero-Usage Rows¶

About 10% of the remaining rows belong to players who dressed for a game but recorded zero targets, carries, or pass attempts. The instinct is to treat these as noise and drop them, but that instinct should be tested, not assumed.

In [ ]:
zero_use = df_clean[(df_clean['attempts']==0)&(df_clean['carries']==0)&(df_clean['targets']==0)]
print(f"Zero-usage rows: {len(zero_use)} ({len(zero_use)/len(df_clean):.1%} of remaining data)")

catchers_used = catchers[catchers['targets']>0]
r_without = catchers_used['targets'].corr(catchers_used['fantasy_points_ppr'])
print(f"targets->PPR correlation WITH zero-usage rows:    r = {r_targets:.3f}")
print(f"targets->PPR correlation WITHOUT zero-usage rows: r = {r_without:.3f}")

Zero-usage rows: 3496 (10.0% of remaining data)
targets->PPR correlation WITH zero-usage rows:    r = 0.806
targets->PPR correlation WITHOUT zero-usage rows: r = 0.778

Removing the zero-usage rows makes the targets-to-points correlation weaker, not stronger (0.806 → 0.778). A zero-touch game legitimately produces a near-zero score. It sits right on the trend line, not off of it. These rows are kept in every analysis that follows. This was the single biggest lesson of the cleaning process: the "obviously safe to drop" rows turned out to support the relationship being tested, not dilute it.

Outliers¶

Are there extreme single-game performances sitting way outside the normal range here, and should they be removed?

In [ ]:
def outlier_share(pos):
    s = df_clean[df_clean['position']==pos]['fantasy_points_ppr']
    q1, q3 = s.quantile([.25,.75])
    iqr = q3-q1
    upper = q3+1.5*iqr
    return (s>upper).sum(), len(s), upper

print("Statistical outliers (>1.5*IQR above Q3) by position:")
for pos in ['QB','RB','WR','TE']:
    n_out, n_tot, cutoff = outlier_share(pos)
    print(f"  {pos}: {n_out} of {n_tot} ({n_out/n_tot:.1%}), upper cutoff = {cutoff:.1f} pts")

Statistical outliers (>1.5*IQR above Q3) by position:
  QB: 10 of 3901 (0.3%), upper cutoff = 40.3 pts
  RB: 222 of 9159 (2.4%), upper cutoff = 27.9 pts
  WR: 421 of 14603 (2.9%), upper cutoff = 26.2 pts
  TE: 280 of 7256 (3.9%), upper cutoff = 18.9 pts
In [ ]:
df_clean.nlargest(5, 'fantasy_points_ppr')[['player_display_name','position','season','week','fantasy_points_ppr']]
Out[ ]:
player_display_name position season week fantasy_points_ppr
Tyreek Hill WR 2020 12 57.9
Alvin Kamara RB 2020 16 56.2
Ja'Marr Chase WR 2021 17 55.6
Ja'Marr Chase WR 2024 10 55.4
Jahmyr Gibbs RB 2025 12 55.4

Decision: keep every statistical outlier. By the standard 1.5×IQR rule, up to 3.9% of TE games and 2.9% of WR games qualify as outliers, hundreds of rows. But naming the top performances shows exactly why removing them would be a mistake: Tyreek Hill's 57.9-point game and Ja'Marr Chase's back-to-back 55-point seasons aren't data errors, they're literally the events fantasy football exists to capture. In this domain, "outlier" and "noise" are not the same thing. The right move isn't to delete the tail, it's to make sure the summary statistics used (median alongside mean) don't get misread because of it. The outlier share itself is also informative and consistent with what comes next: QB has almost none (0.3%) while TE has the most (3.9%).

With the data cleaned (kickers dropped, structural NaNs left alone, zero-usage games retained, no outliers removed), the same summary statistics can be recomputed on data that's actually trustworthy.

df_clean.groupby('position')['fantasy_points_ppr'].agg(

coefficient_of_variation
position
QB 0.670
RB 1.024
WR 1.047
TE 1.080

The boxplot makes the consistency question visible at a glance: QB's box is tighter relative to its own median than any other position, and it has almost no fliers. RB, WR, and TE all show a long tail of outlier dots stretching well above the box. The coefficient of variation puts a number on it: QB (0.67) is clearly the steadiest position; TE (1.08) is the least consistent, which matches the "TE premium" idea a lot of fantasy analysts already hold. A handful of elite tight ends produce most of the position's value, and the drop-off to a replacement-level TE is steep.

Distribution Shape by Position¶

A boxplot compresses the whole distribution into five numbers. Looking at the actual shape confirms whether QB really is more bell-shaped, and whether RB/WR/TE really are that lopsided.

In [ ]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(10,7.5))
positions = ['QB','RB','WR','TE']
colors2 = ['#4C72B0','#DD8452','#55A868','#C44E52']
for ax, pos, c in zip(axes.flat, positions, colors2):
    vals = df_clean[df_clean['position']==pos]['fantasy_points_ppr']
    ax.hist(vals, bins=30, color=c, alpha=0.75, edgecolor='white')
    ax.axvline(vals.mean(), color='black', linestyle='--', linewidth=1, label=f'mean={vals.mean():.1f}')
    ax.axvline(vals.median(), color='gray', linestyle=':', linewidth=1.3, label=f'median={vals.median():.1f}')
    ax.set_title(pos)
    ax.set_xlabel('PPR fantasy points')
    ax.legend(fontsize=8)
fig.suptitle('Distribution Shape of PPR Fantasy Points by Position', y=1.00, fontsize=13)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

This is the clearest picture in the whole notebook. QB is genuinely close to a normal, bell-ish shape, with a real peak away from zero. RB, WR, and TE are all zero-inflated and heavily right-skewed: a huge spike of games near 0–2 points, then a long thinning tail out past 40. That single visual difference explains almost everything else found so far: why the zero-usage rows matter so much for RB/WR/TE but barely register as an issue for QB, and why QB's coefficient of variation is so much lower than the other three positions.

Additional Analysis¶

Player-Level Consistency: Boom or Bust?¶

The position-level numbers say QB is the steadiest position and TE is the least. Whether that holds up at the individual player level can be checked directly by looking at the most consistent and most volatile individual player-seasons among meaningful fantasy starters (10+ games, 10+ PPR points per game average).

In [ ]:
player_season = df_clean.groupby(['player_id','player_display_name','position','season'])['fantasy_points_ppr'].agg(['count','mean','std'])
player_season = player_season[player_season['count'] >= 10]
player_season['cv'] = player_season['std'] / player_season['mean']
relevant = player_season[player_season['mean'] >= 10]
print(f"Player-seasons qualifying (10+ games, 10+ PPR pt average): {len(relevant)}")

It holds up, and then some. Every one of the five most consistent player-seasons in the entire dataset is a quarterback, led by Lamar Jackson's 2024 season (25.3 points/game with a standard deviation of only 6.2). The most volatile list is almost entirely non-QB, and Rashaad Penny's 2021 season is the clearest example of boom-or-bust in the dataset: a 12.2-point average with a 12.5-point standard deviation means his week-to-week swing was roughly the size of his own average, some huge games mixed with quiet or injury-limited ones, rather than a stable role producing a similar stat line every week. Jameis Winston's 2024 season is the one QB exception, which fits his reputation as a genuinely volatile, boom-or-bust passer even by NFL standards.

Team-Level Fantasy Production¶

Individual talent isn't the only factor in fantasy scoring. Offensive scheme and team context matter too. Which teams' skill-position players score the most fantasy points per game on average, and which score the least?

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11,5.5))
colors = ['#4C72B0' if v>=team_avg.median() else '#C44E52' for v in team_avg.values]

ax.set_ylabel('Avg PPR fantasy points per skill-position player-game')

plt.xticks(rotation=90)
ax.legend()
ax.grid(axis='y', alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Detroit's skill players averaged 9.33 PPR points per game across six seasons, nearly 40% higher than Carolina's 6.68, the lowest team in the league. This tracks with real-world reputation (Detroit has run one of the league's best offenses this stretch; Carolina has been near the bottom), which is a good sanity check that the data reflects reality. Practically, this means offensive context is itself a predictive signal. Drafting a mid-tier player from a top-scoring offense is a reasonable way to get upside beyond what an individual talent projection alone would suggest.

Scoring Trends Across Seasons¶

The NFL's offensive strategies shift from year to year. Has average fantasy production at each position actually changed across these six seasons, or has it stayed flat?

In [ ]:

season_trend = season_trend[['QB','RB','WR','TE']]
season_trend.round(2)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8,5.5))
colors_map = {'QB':'#4C72B0','RB':'#DD8452','WR':'#55A868','TE':'#C44E52'}
for pos in ['QB','RB','WR','TE']:
    ax.plot(season_trend.index, season_trend[pos], marker='o', label=pos, color=colors_map[pos])
ax.set_xlabel('Season')
ax.set_ylabel('Avg PPR fantasy points per game')
ax.set_title('Average Fantasy Scoring by Position, 2020–2025')
ax.legend()
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
ax.set_xticks(season_trend.index)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

QB scoring has drifted down since 2020 (14.99 → 13.36 points/game) and WR shows the same pattern, with a noticeable dip in 2025 (6.67, its lowest point in the six-season window). RB and TE have stayed comparatively flat across the whole period. The practical takeaway: don't anchor draft-value expectations to 2020 numbers. The scoring environment for QB and WR specifically has cooled somewhat since then, so a player's percentile rank within his own season matters more than comparing raw point totals across years.

Conclusion¶

This project set out to test a handful of fantasy football assumptions against six real NFL seasons rather than gut feel, using a dataset that was complex and genuinely messy in the ways sports data actually gets messy, not a toy example. A few conclusions came out of it that are worth carrying into an actual draft:

  • Volume of opportunity strongly predicts fantasy production, but it's an opportunity metric, not a production metric. Receiving yards (r = 0.914) correlate tighter with PPR points than targets do (r = 0.806) because yards sit closer to the scoring formula itself, and touchdowns barely correlate with volume at all (0.35–0.44) despite driving a large share of the week-to-week scoring swing.
  • QB is the most consistent fantasy position by a clear margin, both at the position level (coefficient of variation 0.67 vs. 1.02–1.08 for RB/WR/TE) and the individual level: the 5 steadiest player-seasons in six years of data are all quarterbacks. The histogram comparison shows why: QB is close to bell-shaped, while RB/WR/TE are all zero-inflated and heavily right-skewed.
  • Team context matters almost as much as individual talent. Detroit's skill players outscored Carolina's by nearly 40% per game on average across six seasons, which is a strong argument for factoring team offensive quality into draft value, not just the player in isolation.
  • The scoring environment itself has shifted. QB and WR production has trended down since 2020, so raw point totals shouldn't be compared across seasons without adjusting for that drift.
  • The most counter-intuitive lesson came from the cleaning process itself. The "obviously safe to drop" rows (zero-usage games) turned out to support the volume-production relationship rather than dilute it. Cleaning a dataset isn't about deciding what looks messy on sight; it's about testing whether a row is actually distorting the analysis before removing it, and in this case the obvious instinct would have been wrong.

For draft day, this pushes toward valuing target share and snap share heavily for WR/TE evaluation, treating touchdown totals with real skepticism since they're the least predictable part of a stat line, leaning into a top-tier QB's floor since the position is genuinely steadier, and giving some weight to offensive context when comparing similarly talented players. For in-season decisions, the boom-or-bust list built here is a practical bench/start tool: a boom-or-bust archetype is a reasonable high-upside flex play in a must-win week but a poor start when a guaranteed floor is needed, while a name from the consistent-performer list is the safer lock-and-start even in a tough matchup.

If this project were extended further, the natural next steps would be incorporating snap-count and target-share data directly (rather than approximating opportunity with raw counting stats), modeling touchdown regression explicitly, and extending the team-level analysis to account for strength of opposing defenses rather than a simple team average.
